slides.0.title: Sake grades, styles and service
slides.0.subtitle: Grades tell you how much the rice was milled and whether alcohol was added
slides.1.title: Grades
slides.1.highlights.0.title: Junmai and non-junmai
slides.1.highlights.0.content: Junmai uses only rice, koji and water; honjozo, ginjo and daiginjo may include a little brewer’s alcohol to lift aroma and lighten the palate, which does not mean lower quality
slides.1.highlights.1.title: Polishing thresholds
slides.1.highlights.1.content: Honjozo 70% or less, ginjo 60% or less, daiginjo 50% or less (the same for junmai ginjo and junmai daiginjo); junmai itself currently has no polishing threshold
slides.1.highlights.2.title: Futsu-shu
slides.1.highlights.2.content: Sake that does not meet the special-designation criteria; the largest volume and affordable, and not all of it is poor; plenty is good for everyday drinking
slides.1.content: Memory aid: honjozo 70, ginjo 60, daiginjo 50; “junmai” only means no added alcohol.
slides.2.title: Styles and service
slides.2.highlights.0.title: Common styles
slides.2.highlights.0.content: Nigori (coarsely filtered, cloudy with lees), genshu (undiluted), namazake (unpasteurised), koshu (long-aged, with caramel and nutty notes)
slides.2.highlights.1.title: Temperature
slides.2.highlights.1.content: Ginjo and daiginjo are usually served chilled to keep their fragrance; junmai, honjozo, kimoto and yamahai can be warmed (kanzake) to round out the rice umami and acidity
slides.2.highlights.2.title: SMV and pairing
slides.2.highlights.2.content: Sake meter value (SMV) is positive for drier and negative for sweeter, though acidity also shapes perception; sake’s umami and low acidity suit seafood, sushi and umami-rich dishes
slides.2.content: Order for recommending sake: style (ginjo or junmai) → temperature → reason for the pairing.
